en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Turning in Accordance with [Reality] and the Proclamation of All Dharmas, Scroll One.
Translated by Imperial Decree by the Śramaṇa Shao De and others, Tripiṭaka Master and Dharma Master of Mingjiao, Biancai, during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
and an assembly of two thousand great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose names were as follows:

They were headed by such bodhisattvas as Adorned Bodhisattva, Lion’s Play Bodhisattva, Immovable Light Bodhisattva, Joyful Stainless Light Bodhisattva, Sunlight Flame Bodhisattva, Profoundly Deep Stainless Bodhisattva, Lotus Mark Bodhisattva, Lion Wisdom Bodhisattva, Golden-Colored Mark Bodhisattva, Brahma-Sound Bodhisattva, Lion-Wisdom King Bodhisattva, Stainless Golden Light Bodhisattva, Subtle and Wondrous Form Body Bodhisattva, Radiating Light to Destroy Māra Bodhisattva, Tranquil Faculties Bodhisattva, Dhāraṇī King Bodhisattva, Auspicious Pure Mark Bodhisattva, and Mañjuśrī Who Subdues and Destroys Māra Bodhisattva.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, amidst the great assembly, beheld the Buddha’s body, its golden hue radiating with brilliance. A heart of love and joy arose within him, and he immediately rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke these verses:

“The Tathāgata’s true golden color, His body adorned with marks and signs of excellence— Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, He has accumulated all manner of meritorious virtues.”
With merit and wisdom both fully perfected, you have realized the unsurpassed path.
Arising with great compassion, you manifest within the Sahā world;
the humans, devas, and the eight classes of beings gaze upon you without ever being satiated.
From within the very nature of reality, the subtle and wondrous Dharma is proclaimed;
it is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom, known only by the Buddha.
Sentient beings, however, are dull-witted and deluded; though they hear this teaching, they cannot understand it.
The Tathāgata, the Great Guide, Is skillful in his expedient means;
He leads those various deluded multitudes To gradual awakening.
The wondrous, luminous mind of sentient beings Is originally and eternally serene and still.
Pure and free from defilement, Endowed with all virtues;
Its essence is like space, Without any obstruction;
Neither arising nor ceasing, Neither going nor coming.
Abiding securely in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), unmoving like Mount Sumeru,
all things are entirely equal— true and inconceivable.
Since beginningless eons, sentient beings have been greedily attached to various desires.
Falling into the ocean of suffering, they are unable to seek liberation.
The Tathāgata’s profound Dharma is subtle and extremely difficult to conceive;
for those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities, he teaches in accordance with their needs.
Just as the single-flavored rain from heaven Pours everywhere throughout the ten directions,
Upon the grasses, trees, and thickets— Whether roots or stems, great or small—
Within the vast expanse of the earth, There is none that does not receive nourishment and benefit.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is likewise entirely so:
with a single subtle and wondrous voice, he expounds immeasurable meanings;
though the faculties and capacities differ, each who hears it attains understanding.
Therefore, within a single assembly, all have entered the Buddha’s wisdom;
this is the power of the Buddha’s spiritual penetrations, called "inconceivable.
Throughout kalpas of the past, I have constantly followed the Buddha’s transformations.
Now, within this assembly, I too am seated beneath the Buddha;
whatever Dharma the Tathāgata preaches, I am able to retain it all in its entirety.
For both the present and the future, I pray that the Buddha will proclaim it for me.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Good son!

The wondrous, luminous, primordial mind of all sentient beings in the world is originally pure and free from all defilements. It is perfectly complete throughout the ten directions, profoundly still and tranquil, like empty space which is fundamentally free from dust and obscuration—serene and pure."
The eye-disease of sentient beings gives rise to flowers in the sky; these flowers arise and perish, seen only by diseased eyes.
Once the cataract of the eye has vanished, the flowers in the sky also cease; the pure void is, from the beginning, unmoving.
The wondrously luminous, original mind is likewise thus: fundamentally pure and free from all defilements.
Sentient beings, however, are inverted; they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses.

Within the various sensory realms, the mind of discrimination arises: the eyes see forms, the ears hear sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the tongue tastes flavors, the body experiences tangibles, and the mind cognizes mental objects.

These six faculties and their respective consciousnesses each pair with their various sensory objects; through deluded conceptualization and attachment to these objects, they give rise to craving and defilement, thereby creating all manner of karma.
Once karma is formed, one undergoes retribution and falls into the ocean of suffering, transmigrating through birth and death and enduring great anguish without rest, like a whirling firebrand.

The Tathāgata, out of great compassion and pity for all beings, has established various skillful means to teach the dharma-gates of śamatha, samāpatti, and dhyāna—namely, the methods of cessation and contemplation—so that they may gather their minds and gradually practice cultivation until they realize the fruit of Buddhahood and escape these evil paths.
“Good son! All ācāryas, for the sake of all sentient beings in the world who seek bodhi, employ a mind of truth and proceed directly upon the right path;
if their mental conduct is stained by desire, crooked, and insincere, then to seek bodhi while practicing such a deviant path is impossible.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who practice wholesome deeds with their minds, eliminate those deluded conceptions, and are free from all discrimination; who realize that phenomena are empty and quiescent, yet harbor no view of emptiness, no view of wishlessness, do not give rise to deluded views, and have no view of intrinsic nature, no view of marks, no view of a Buddha, and no view of Bodhi; who constantly practice right view, plant various roots of goodness, and fulfill their vows for Bodhi—such persons are like priceless jewels.”
Furthermore, all Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—have practiced this path and thereby attained Bodhi, which is called liberation.
Having utterly severed doubt and the mind of non-discrimination, they purify their verbal karma by preaching the True Dharma;

they attain all-knowledge and manifest the mark of spontaneity, manifesting that which is neither word nor non-word. They preach the mark of reality, and preach the mark of the bodhicitta: they preach generosity because it is equanimity and free from greed; they preach ethical discipline because it is free from all defiled desires; they preach patience because the mind is free from resentment; they preach diligence because it is free from all indolence; they preach meditative concentration because it dwells in tranquility; and they preach wisdom because it is well able to discern.
In this way, he individually expounded upon the gates of śamatha, samāpatti, and dhyāna—hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of gates, profound and beyond compare.

The sentient beings dwelling in the peripheral hells, upon hearing the sound of the Dharma being preached, were all liberated from the various evil realms; they realized emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and attained liberation.

Thus, through reverent offerings and the purification of the three karmas, they honored his merit and attained peace of mind as if upon level ground. All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas day and night revere this profound liberation as the most supreme and foremost.
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita praised and rejoiced, gaining profound understanding.
At that time, the Blessed One—
And he spoke in verse:
“Between you and the world, and all sentient beings, there is no duality of mind;
by realizing that all phenomena are empty, you have attained bodhi.”
Do not allow [them] to arise again; self-nature is pure, and false imaginings do not occur.
With a mind of equality and single-mindedness, there is no distraction.
In such an assembly as this, contemplate all things as illusions and dreams;
by realizing they are not real, you shall proceed toward the Bodhi of the Buddha, certain that it is not far off.
Having attained such a path, there is attainment yet no attainment; there is clarity yet no clarity—this alone accords with the Tathāgata.
With wisdom clearly manifest, knowing in this manner, one is foremost in the world;
named a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa), all people revere and honor him.
Beginning with the turning of the mind toward enlightenment, one draws near to virtuous friends, gazing upon and serving them without any indolence.
Gradually advancing, one realizes that the nature of all phenomena is empty;
by diligently cultivating all practices without further regression, one is born in a superior realm and attains bodhi.
When meditative concentration manifests, it is profoundly still and unmoving;
there is neither the observance of precepts nor conceptual discrimination between having precepts and lacking them, for their essential nature is one.
Having attained Bodhi, their minds enter the Buddha-vehicle;
they dwell securely in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), their essence like empty space, free from all obstruction.
They expound the True Dharma to deliver all sentient beings, maintaining an impartial and single mind, no different from the Buddhas.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who are greedily attached to negligence and do not study the Noble Path;
their bodies and minds are distracted, just like madmen or sorcerers,
constantly committing the grave offenses of the three poisons day and night.
Fools are cruel and evil, their natures difficult to subdue; being utterly deluded, they ultimately gain no benefit.
Associating with evil friends, they are addicted to the five desires and infatuated with women, never relinquishing them for even a moment.
With single-minded intent, that person commits the offense of breaking the precepts; in their folly they remain unaware, utterly destroying their *śīla*.
Among those who break the precepts, this is the foremost; regarding all wholesome paths, there is not even a hair’s breadth remaining.
Those who zealously practice as icchantikas, harboring resentment and arrogance, shall undergo bitter retribution once they have completed their commission of sins.
Having no fondness for any wholesome dharmas, they leap for joy upon hearing the sound of music, their hearts clinging to it without letting go.
Associating with evil people, their bodies and speech were unwholesome;
following along with greed and hatred, they took pleasure together and gradually traveled on until they reached a village.
In that village, many people practice virtue;
yet they do not give rise to reverence, but instead seek out evil friends, together creating sensual pleasures,
falling into the evil realms, and losing the path to Bodhi.
A bhikṣu who is a true kinsman, having performed various meritorious deeds and seeking the practice of the Mahāyāna,
does not delight in associating with those who hear the sounds of the Lesser Dharma.
Free from pride, he traveled afar to seek out Dharma masters;
he diligently sought the sublime Dharma and upheld dhāraṇīs and secret verses.
He transcribed hundreds of thousands of countless sutra scrolls; his wisdom shone forth, and he leaped for joy.
Such a person attains the merit of a Buddha and is no different from a Buddha;
for even throughout ten million *koṭi* eons, they shall never again regress, dwelling securely in the Buddha-way,
serene and unmoving.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having now heard the profound and wondrous Dharma spoken by the Buddha, we have attained what we have never experienced before; our hearts are filled with joy. Beholding your majestic radiance and reverently upholding your compassionate instructions, we vow to diligently cultivate ourselves without daring to be indolent, and shall expound the teachings for those who delight in the Dharma according to their needs.”

At that time, there were also devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, together with their retinues and the beings of the world, who all came to approach, make offerings, pay homage, revere, and prostrate, all seeking liberation.
Furthermore, eight thousand sons of gods, together with their retinues, abandoned celestial pleasures and came to the Buddha’s dwelling to hear the sublime Dharma and seek liberation.
Additionally, two thousand yakṣas, together with their retinues, cast off their violence and wickedness, and all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there were three thousand great nāgas who, together with their retinues, gave rise to the bodhicitta and came to the Buddha’s presence, seeking liberation.

Additionally, there was an assembly of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who all came to approach him, paying homage with reverence and prostration, honoring and praising him with joyful exultation, as they listened to and received his teachings while seeking the path to bodhi.
Moreover, there was an assembly of two thousand koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on the Dharma, were freed from hindrances and attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, saying: "Good son!

In the past, you and I, in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, heard the essential teachings on the Dharma and practiced the path of patience. We dwelt peacefully in the endurance of suffering without any transgression; no evil arose, and we were fully perfected."

Furthermore, they heard the exposition of the six pāramitās—namely, the pāramitā of giving, the pāramitā of ethical discipline, the pāramitā of patience, the pāramitā of diligence, the pāramitā of meditative concentration, and the pāramitā of wisdom—and by means of this, they heard the most supreme and wondrous Dharma, whereby their roots of goodness increased and they attained non-retrogression.
Because at that time you heard the Buddha’s Dharma, practiced with diligent effort, realized the fruits of the Path, and attained the marks of a Great Man;

you shall always revere the Buddha-Dharma, constantly make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, serve spiritual friends, realize the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, and bring forth right mindfulness.

“Good son! Furthermore, in the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Sumeru-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
The lifespan of that Buddha was immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years, and his world was named Lapis Lazuli Golden Light.

The ground of that Buddha-land was as level as a whetstone, adorned with a combination of various jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, and agate—and was free from all impurities, rubble, and thorns.

“Good son! At that time, within that Buddha’s assembly, there were eight hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats; their outflows were exhausted, they were free from all fetters and afflictions, and their minds had attained liberation.
Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of bhikṣuṇīs.”
Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of assemblies of upāsakas and countless hundreds of thousands of assemblies of upāsikās who all came together for this gathering.
"O son of good family!
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to transform and guide sentient beings of the three vehicles:

for the śrāvakas, he taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; for the pratyekabuddhas, he taught the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and for the bodhisattvas, he taught the Dharma of the Six Pāramitās.
Through these most profound and subtle essentials of all wholesome dharmas, he caused the great assembly to dwell securely within the Dharma, each attaining liberation.

“Good son! At that time, the ground of jewels in that world of Lapis Lazuli Golden Light was level and even. Many jewel trees stood in rows along the sides of the roads, which were demarcated by golden cords and interlaced with nets of jewels. When a gentle breeze blew, they brushed against one another, producing subtle and wondrous sounds;

those sounds proclaimed the various sublime Dharma-sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—namely, the sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of non-arising, the sound of non-ceasing, the sound of formlessness, and the sound of lack of intrinsic nature.”
The sentient beings therein, hearing these various subtle and wondrous sounds, felt joy arise in their hearts and each attained liberation. "Good son!

Within the pure Dharma of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sumerurāja, you shall become a bhikṣu named Prajñācodaka; you will love and delight in the True Dharma and seek the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes."

Free from all craving and desire, with the root of their precepts pure, their minds are constantly joyful as they praise the Mahāyāna; day and night they practice diligently, paying respectful homage and making offerings.

When others come seeking the Dharma, they expound it for them accordingly, giving rise to no stinginess, explaining it in various ways to bring about their liberation. Their minds are free from seeking, dwelling in equanimity, fully endowed with roots of goodness, and fulfilling their vows for Bodhi.
“Good son! At that time, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, that bhikṣu delighted in reciting the sūtras, increasing his wisdom, and taking refuge in the immeasurable merits of the Mahāyāna;
furthermore, he served his ācāryas and kalyāṇamitras, making offerings to them throughout the kalpa without ever becoming weary.”
Employing many skillful means, he brings peace and happiness to all. "Good son!
That Bhikṣu Prajñā-praśaṃsaka, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, abandoned his former dwelling and traveled through various villages, going from door to door in succession to beg for food."
Among them, there were male and female lay followers of pure faith who came to attend upon him, giving rise to a heart of reverence and respect, and making various kinds of offerings;

they exhorted the Bhikṣu Prajñākūṭa to preach the essentials of the Dharma, and through his immeasurable merit in patience and meditative concentration, he caused them to attain faith and understanding, strengthening their resolve for the Path.
Within that village, there was another class of inferior sentient beings who, upon seeing the Sangha, were struck with terror; they took no pleasure in the sight of them and fled far away.
Due to the causal conditions of their past evil karma, they were no different from birds or beasts.

At that time, the bhikṣu Quanhui, seeing those wicked people, gave rise to a heart of compassion; undaunted by hardship, he gradually drew near to them, exhorting, instructing, and guiding them by preaching the essentials of the Dharma, until each of them examined themselves, repented their transgressions, and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
“Good son! At that time, the elder friends and spiritual mentors who resided in the monastery with the bhikṣu Prajñākūṭa said to one another:
‘That bhikṣu Prajñākūṭa has planted roots of goodness in past lives and profoundly mastered the essentials of the Dharma; he serves as the foremost leader among this assembly.’”
"For what reason have you now abandoned this monastery to travel far into the villages, undergoing extreme hardship to teach and transform sentient beings while wandering for alms?
We bhikṣus have been filled with longing thoughts; we have come together to go far out and invite you to return."
Upon arriving there, they saw Kuānhuì from afar and were all filled with joy; each of them greeted him, asking:
"Are you light and agile in your movements?
Are you dwelling in well-being and peace?"

We have come from afar to seek you out; we pray that you will return to your former dwelling, where we shall provide you with exquisite food and drink, incense, flowers, lamps, and fruits, at the proper times, without fail for a long duration.
We only pray that, out of compassion, you will return together to your old abode.
At that time, the bhikṣu Prajñāpradīpa did not accept his invitation, for he delighted in dwelling in tranquility.

He again left the village and traveled far away, where he encountered a forest hermitage (araṇya). There, casting aside all worldly attachments, he dwelt in profound stillness, diligently practicing asceticism, accumulating merit, and causing the seed of omniscience to grow ever more radiant.

At another time, the bhikṣu Quanhui, no longer finding joy in the araṇya, entered once more into deep mountains where no humans could reach. He marveled at how this environment was fit for peaceful dwelling, and he observed the summer retreat with diligent discipline, practicing meditative contemplation in accordance with the Buddha’s prohibitions.

Furthermore, many wild beasts within this place—tigers, wolves, lions, jackals, and birds—all came to draw near, carrying flowers in their beaks and offering fruits, performing various kinds of worship.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prajñācitta felt great joy and became even more diligent and energetic, without any regression. "Good son!

In a past age, there was a class of bhikṣus who felt no love or joy for the Buddha’s teachings; they did not cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), nor did they protect their ethical discipline (śīla). They slandered the Mahāyāna, consumed the offerings of the faithful in vain, lacked shame and remorse, distanced themselves from spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and constantly associated with evil people."
Those with superior-grade greed and poison are avoided by all; through folly and evil deeds, they lose their monastic robes.

Having fallen into hell, they undergo great suffering for ninety *koṭi* hundreds of thousands of *kalpas*. Once these offenses are exhausted, they further undergo the most extreme suffering among sufferings for sixty hundred thousand *koṭi* *kalpas*, beyond all comparison.

Later, he encountered the bhikṣu Quanhui, who provided various expositions and taught him the pure vehicle of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, causing him to give rise to faith and understanding.

“Good son! The bhikṣu named Prajñā-praśaṃsaka, as well as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, was also a bhikṣu within that Dharma. He delighted in the True Dharma and sought the wisdom of the Buddha; with a sincere mind, he made offerings and showed reverence, honoring the Buddha-Dharma, transcribing the sūtras, and performing various meritorious deeds without any indolence of heart.

Associating with spiritual friends and employing many skillful means, he gave rise to a joyful mind to exhort and transform sentient beings, causing them all to attain liberation; at that time, all living beings were filled with joy and looked up to him with veneration.”
“Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata further expounded the essentials of all dharmas for the bhikṣu Prajñā-praśamsita, causing him to increase his cultivation of the knowledge of all modes;

so that suffering and affliction would not arise, greed and anger would not be committed, he would not follow evil friends to fall into the various evil realms, and he would protect himself from all faults. With a single mind, he made offerings to and preached the True Dharma, constantly upholding the pure jewel of the Dharma day and night, gradually advancing without ever regressing.”
“Good son! At that time, the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm, having heard what the Buddha taught, practiced the ten wholesome actions and dwelt securely within the Dharma;
all bodhisattvas practiced the six pāramitās, perfected their merits, and brought peace and happiness to all.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, saying:
"The bhikṣu Prajñācodaka of that time was none other than you yourself.

The Sūtra on the Exposition of All Dharmas According with the Mahāyāna Spoken by the Buddha, Middle Volume.

At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does one eliminate karmic obstacles and attain a pure mind?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“To be free from evil karma, one should study all dharmas and understand that the discrimination of all dharmas arises from the mind and is empty, false, and unreal.
When the wisdom of emptiness manifests before one, karmic obstacles are naturally eliminated, and the mind attains purity.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
All sentient beings, since beginningless kalpas, have been deluded by false imaginings and inversions, taking greed, anger, and ignorance as their three causes.

They have committed immeasurable and boundless karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, falling into various realms and transmigrating through birth and death, undergoing great suffering and affliction without rest. Because their karmic obstructions are intense and evil demons harass them, their minds cannot attain purity."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If you now wish to know how all sentient beings may be freed from all karmic obstructions and attain purity of mind,
they should study all the dharmas of the Tathāgata, purify their three karmas of body, speech, and mind, and apply themselves with diligence day and night."
Practicing the holy life, remaining far removed from suffering and affliction, with non-arising through discernment, aspiring for bodhi,
reverently making offerings to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, reciting and practicing Mahāyāna sūtras and secret dhāraṇīs for a long time,
possessing firmness of body and mind without regression, contemplating and understanding [the nature of] arising and abiding.
Differing in their cessation, they are impermanent from moment to moment, arising and perishing in every instant; all are false and devoid of reality.
Abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one gradually progresses, the mind free from distraction, so that no evil Māras can find an opportunity.
Spontaneous joy arises, the mental ground becomes illuminated, and accumulated merits flourish and grow.
O Āyuṣmat, you have realized the fruit of the unsurpassed path of Buddha-bodhi;
this is called renunciation, and you are a true son of the Buddha.
You now know that the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma is as vast as the ocean, benefiting sentient beings without end.

Having attained the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure, they further cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Free from all suffering and affliction, they obtain the power of merit, practice equanimity, and constantly guard and maintain their minds. Day and night, they revere, respect, and praise [the Dharma], attaining complete liberation and experiencing joy in both body and mind.

Fully understanding that all arising and ceasing are nothing but illusions and dreams, they abide within the Dharma, are born in superior realms, and, being perfectly complete, never again undergo decline.
"By practicing in this way, evil karma is naturally eliminated and the mind attains purity.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the Four Noble Truths?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The Four Noble Truths refer to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; these are called the Four Noble Truths."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one study?”
The Buddha said:
"One should study all dharmas so that the wisdom of those dharmas manifests before one;
therein, no discrimination arises regarding what is wholesome or unwholesome. One contemplates the self-nature of all things as pure and understands that everything is entirely illusory."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How is it that all sentient beings do not train?
The Buddha said:

“Foolish ordinary beings, in order to slander the teachings, do not give rise to wholesome thoughts, do not cultivate the holy life, do not read or recite the scriptures, do not accept instruction, and are unwilling to study even a little of the Buddha’s Dharma;

they constantly commit evil deeds and take delight in wandering through the three realms, failing to realize that all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, and like mirages—empty, false, and unreal.”

If all sentient beings study all wholesome dharmas, cultivate the samādhi of śamatha, contemplate the intrinsic purity of self-nature, and realize that desire, hatred, and ignorance are entirely illusory, they will abide in the Dharma, attain that power of concentration, and experience bliss of body and mind.
“Fools do not study the wholesome dharmas; they do not know that there exist the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, which pervade all of space and are subtle and difficult to perceive.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way is this dharma so subtle that sentient beings find it difficult to see?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"This Dharma is like wind giving rise to waves; one sees only the rising of the waves but does not see the arising of the wind.
Only you, Mañjuśrī, and Subhūti can understand this; all others do not comprehend it."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?”
The Buddha said:

“Mañjuśrī! The four foundations of mindfulness consist of contemplating the body as impure, contemplating feelings as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as selfless; these are called the four foundations of mindfulness.”
Mañjuśrī asked, “How should one train?
The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings should contemplate their own five kinds of impurity;
they should contemplate that among feelings there are three—painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neutral feeling—all of which are suffering;
and they should contemplate that the mind is impermanent, impermanent from moment to moment, arising and ceasing in every instant."
Contemplating the non-self of phenomena, one sees that the four great elements and the five aggregates have no real essence of self;
this is called the four foundations of mindfulness,
and all sentient beings should train in this manner.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the five faculties?”
"They are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; these are called the five faculties.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "How should one train in them?"
The Buddha said:

"For sentient beings who train in the Dharma, because they contemplate this dharma as profound and far-reaching within all dharmas and are thus able to give rise to faith, it is called the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya).
Because they thoroughly understand this dharma and practice with diligent vigor to eliminate hindrances and attain liberation, it is called the faculty of diligence (vīryendriya)."
In this regard, to single-mindedly contemplate and keep this Dharma in mind without forgetting is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*);
to clearly know that all phenomena are necessarily produced from the mind is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*);
and to discern with wisdom that all phenomena are empty is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
"These are called the five faculties.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the seven factors of enlightenment?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"The factor of mindfulness, the factor of discrimination of phenomena, the factor of energy, the factor of joy, the factor of tranquility, the factor of concentration, and the factor of equanimity—these are called the seven factors of enlightenment."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one train?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"For sentient beings training in the Dharma, to thoroughly understand all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena within their own nature, to abandon worldly conditions, and to diligently attend to the true Dharma—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness."
"Discernment" (vīmaṃsā) refers to the ability to discern within the three realms by means of intrinsic wisdom; thus it is called the factor of enlightenment of discernment.
"Diligence" (viriya) refers to the thorough understanding of all phenomena and their persistent practice without abandonment; thus it is called the factor of enlightenment of diligence.

"Joy" (pīti) refers to the arising of delight regarding all conditioned formations, and the experience of the blissful nature of sublime qualities through joyful practice day and night; thus it is called the factor of enlightenment of joy.
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) refers to abiding peacefully within all phenomena without being disturbed by Māra, whereby the mind attains mastery; thus it is called the awakening factor of pliancy.
Concentration (*samādhi*) refers to realizing that all phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic nature and cultivating *samādhi*; this is called the awakening factor of concentration.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) refers to the mind abiding peacefully in all phenomena, neither dwelling on wisdom nor dwelling on the Buddha, and relinquishing all conditions; this is called the awakening factor of equanimity.
"These are called the seven factors of enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the Eightfold Noble Path?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are called the Eightfold Noble Path."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one train?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“When all those sentient beings thoroughly understand all dharmas and pay reverence through the three karmas, this is called right view;
when they, regarding all dharmas, engage in discrimination or non-discrimination, and experience joy or lack of joy, this is called right thought.”
To thoroughly understand all phenomena and speak with truth is called right speech;
to thoroughly understand that among all phenomena one performs only wholesome deeds is called right action;
to abide in the mind of equanimity regarding all phenomena is called right livelihood.
To diligently cultivate the Mahāyāna regarding all phenomena is called right effort;
to not give rise to unwholesome karma regarding all phenomena is called right mindfulness;
and to be neither distracted nor disordered regarding all phenomena is called right concentration.
This is called the Eightfold Noble Path.

Those sentient beings who study the Dharma single-mindedly comprehend the Four Noble Truths, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, the Five Faculties, the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, and the Eightfold Noble Path. Having practiced and studied each of these dharmas, they reach the other shore, are born in the lands of the Buddhas, are free from all fear, and attain the adamantine, steadfast mind.

All arhats, śrāvakas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and minor brāhmaṇas, upon hearing the Buddha preach this subtle and supreme dharma-gate, will possess great spiritual power, be able to eliminate their feverish afflictions, and attain the coolness of the mind-ground;
if these bhikṣus can practice it diligently from one to another with minds that never regress, they will be no different from me.

Furthermore, the devas and humans play various kinds of music day and night, and they present numerous sublime incenses, diverse and wondrous flowers, and exquisite foods and drinks, all worthy of being offered as sustenance.

“Mañjuśrī! If those bhikṣus do not sever their anger, yet enter royal cities with their alms bowls to wander for food, they will be tormented by Māra; becoming attached to various desires, they are not disciples of the Buddha and are no different from worldly people.”

Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who, because their minds are free from anger, thoroughly understand the subtle and wondrous practice of the Dharma, the meaning of the Dharma, and its words and phrases; they thereby attain liberation through true and correct practice.

At that time, three thousand two hundred devaputras, holding celestial māndārava flowers, various kinds of famous incenses, and exquisite food and drink, made offerings with deep reverence. Their hearts were filled with great joy as they praised one another for the merit of leaving the household life, saying it was no different from that of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-land.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What are the secret dhāraṇī verses and phrases that I have heard the Buddha proclaim?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“I shall explain for you the secret phrases, the wedge-phrases, the vajra-phrases, and the wisdom-phrases; these are called the dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī chapters and verses.”
"In this Dharma-gate, a bodhisattva attains the arising of all dharma-phrases and attains the dharma of patience moment by moment.
Mañjuśrī asked, "What is called the Dharma-gate of the Secret Phrases?"
The Buddha said:
"I shall explain for you the secret phrases and the true verses. Among all dharmas, the mind’s delight in secret phrases is foremost;
just as you, Mañjuśrī, are foremost among all bodhisattvas, so too are these secret phrases."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

The secret phrase is like space; my body pervades space, and all dharmas likewise pervade space. All bodhisattvas, whether manifest or unmanifest, are one and the same suchness (*tathatā*); this is called the true secret phrase.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is the 'stake-word'?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“I shall explain for you the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada): not moving from the dharma-realm of desire, yet abiding in the movement of all dharmas;
not moving from the Great Vehicle, yet not engaging in various worldly affairs—this is called the stake-word.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the vajra-word?”
The Buddha said:
"I shall explain for you the vajra-phrase: 'Sentient beings harbor anger for a long time,' yet the vajra can sever all phenomena; this is called the vajra-phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the phrase of wisdom?”
The Buddha said:
"I shall explain for you the phrases of wisdom: ignorance is the training in the Buddha's knowledge; all sentient beings who do not train in the Buddha's knowledge will not reach the other shore."

If sentient beings study the Buddha’s wisdom and become fully endowed with all forms of insight, such that they can thoroughly understand both those who possess wisdom and those who do not—this is profound. Mañjuśrī!
"To be able to fully understand that sentient beings lack wisdom, take pleasure only in various evils, and are unable to distance themselves from all phenomena—this is called a secret phrase.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the consciousness of secret phrases?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"Consciousness is like an illusion or a transformation; it falsely gives rise to all phenomena. They are empty and lack intrinsic nature or self-characteristics. Thus, the five aggregates are like five fingers—unreal like space—and are all merely provisional designations."
“Sentient beings are dazed and bewildered, unable to understand; this is called a ‘secret phrase.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What is the secret phrase regarding form?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “Form is all dharmas;
sentient beings are deluded in mind and deluded in eye, slandering the True Dharma and not delighting in diligent study. They crave and take pleasure in form, not knowing it is illusory.”
“Mañjuśrī! You are able to fully comprehend all sensory objects of form; this is called a secret phrase.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the sound of the secret phrase?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The arising of sound is empty and cannot be perceived; the various sounds of speech and resonance are received by the auditory consciousness—this is called a secret phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the fragrance of the secret phrases?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"Fragrance arises from various particles and cannot be seen; it is merely that which consciousness perceives through hearing. Since consciousness itself is non-existent, all of this is illusory. This is called a secret phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of the secret phrases?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Taste has no intrinsic nature; it arises falsely in the tongue. Sentient beings discriminate it, delighting in it and becoming greedily attached to it—this is called a secret phrase.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the touch of the secret phrases?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"Because contact is fundamentally non-existent, one should contemplate all phenomena as being like space. Sentient beings, deluded and confused, become variously attached to objects and the body, regarding them as exquisite contacts; this is called a secret phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the stage of the secret phrases?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"The nature of the earth is substantial and real; when one contemplates phenomena, they lack intrinsic nature and possess no self-characteristics. Yet sentient beings, through inversion, falsely cling to them as existing and become attached to them in various ways—this is called a secret phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the secret phrase of water?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“To contemplate the nature of all waters as being like a mirage, because they are false and unreal—this is called a secret phrase.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the fire of the secret syllable?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"The nature of fire is fierce and brings suffering to sentient beings; because this dharma is extinguished, its self-nature is quiescent, conceptualization does not arise, and it is the supreme, ultimate bliss—this is called a secret phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the wind of the secret phrases?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Wind is entirely unobservable among all phenomena; yet sentient beings are greedily attached to movement and coming-and-going, being turned by the power of the wind—this is called a secret phrase.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the secret phrases are likewise for the Buddha?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All unwholesome dharmas are each explained and taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions to instruct and transform sentient beings; this is called a secret phrase.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that the dharma of secret phrases is also like this?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"All phenomena are neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned;
to contemplate that they are without self, without intrinsic characteristics, and without intrinsic nature, with a mind that is undistracted—this is called the secret phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the Sangha of secret phrases is also like this?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“Those who dwell in the countless sublime dharmadhātu, who maintain the precepts with equanimity within samādhi, and cultivate equanimous wisdom and equanimous liberation—because they are well-established in the dharma of equanimity, there is nothing further for them to learn; this is called a secret phrase.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the stake-sentence of the realm of space?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"All dharmas are the realm of emptiness and the realm of the inconceivable; within all realms they cannot be grasped, cannot be relinquished, and cannot be dwelt upon, for there is no place of dwelling. This is called the 'Pile-Point' (kīla-pada)."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ by which all dharmas abide in space?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All phenomena do not depart from abiding in empty space; because they do not give rise to afflictions and abide in tranquility, this is called the ‘stake-word.’”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ regarding the non-discriminating mind of all dharmas?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“All dharmas are not studied, not inquired about, not performed, not cultivated, not aspired toward, and do not give rise to attachment; they are quiescent like space—this is called the ‘Pile-Pin’ (kīla) phrase.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in what sense is the ‘nail-word’ (kīla-pada) regarding all phenomena subtle?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“All phenomena are free from defilement, abiding in purity; they are the wondrous, perfect, and pure sovereignty of light, the perfect and pure emptiness of space, and the arising of the subtle and marvelous. When the body abides in the Dharma, this is called the ‘Pillar Statement’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is this ‘nail-sentence’ by which all phenomena abide in empty space?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All phenomena abide in emptiness and are invisible; all phenomena abide free from defilement and are likewise invisible. This is called the ‘Pillar Statement’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) for the instruction and study of all dharmas?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“To teach all dharmas to sentient beings while they do not come forward to study diligently, do not learn to practice visualization, do not apply their minds, and do not study during the six periods of day and night; furthermore, they do not question those seated beside them, do not gather for explanations, cannot proclaim the teachings, lack wisdom, and cannot discern them; moreover, they have no love for the teachings, do not associate with virtuous friends, and are arrogant and conceited—being thus far removed from instruction and failing to attain liberation—this is called the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) that is the supreme transcendence of all phenomena?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"All sentient beings are unwilling to study the various wholesome dharmas; they only commit evil deeds, do not associate with the virtuous and good, and possess no wisdom. This is called the 'stake-word'."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
why is it that sentient beings are difficult to instruct through the 'stake-word'?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If sentient beings do not allow their minds to be distracted, but instead diligently study the Dharma, drawing near to and making offerings to it, and naturally approach those who teach and seek the Dharma, then merit and wisdom will arise.
If sentient beings do not study any of the dharmas but only create evil karma, seeking merit and wisdom will be impossible; this is called the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do sentient beings attain all-knowledge through the phrase of the wedge?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All sentient beings who diligently seek and study the Dharma attain all-knowledge;
those who give rise to a heart of joy and practice the Mahāyāna path, clearly understanding their own nature, attain all-knowledge—this is called the ‘Pile-Point’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do sentient beings obtain the fulfillment of the wisdom of all-knowledge through the ‘stake-word’?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“The intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is, within that very intrinsic nature, equal to the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing wisdom; to fully understand that they are of one and the same essence and characteristic—this is called the ‘Pile-Pin’ (kīla) statement.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) that constitutes the bodhimanda for all sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is solely the seeking of the Buddha-dharma; it is the site of the tranquility of all dharmas, the site of the nature of all dharmas, and the site of the seeking of all dharmas.”
Mañjuśrī! Regarding what is called the bodhimanda, I seek the Dharma with a single mind and do not seek any other signs;
that all sentient beings and all people always delight in going there to seek this bodhimanda—this is called the "stake-word" (kīla-pada).
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do all sentient beings attain this patience through the phrase of the stake?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"When sentient beings who study the Dharma cease discursive thought and practice contemplation, pure wisdom arises; they no longer give rise to discrimination regarding names and signs and attain the equanimity of patience—this is called the 'Pile Stake' (kīla-pada)."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) by which all sentient beings are taught the Dharma by their virtuous friends?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"When all sentient beings, along with the devas and humans of the ten directions and the various minor devas, each preach the Dharma, aspiring for Bodhi, their hearts giving rise to joy, making offerings and showing reverence, eliminating hindrances with equanimity, and abiding in the absence of substantial characteristics—this is called the 'Pile-Post' (kīla) phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do all sentient beings obtain this dhāraṇī through the ‘stake-word’?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All sentient beings study the contemplation of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
they maintain profound, perfect discrimination and perfect non-discrimination—this is called the ‘nail-word’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that the stake-sentence (kīla-pada) is fully endowed with the mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"When all sentient beings delight in cultivating a mind of loving-kindness, thoroughly understand all phenomena, and attain impartial loving-kindness, this is called the 'Pile Stake' (kīla) phrase."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ by which all sentient beings are fully endowed with a heart of compassion?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All sentient beings who diligently study the Tathāgata’s mind of equal great compassion and become fully endowed with the essence of great compassion—this is called the ‘Pile Driver’ phrase.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ by which all sentient beings do not attain samādhi?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “All sentient beings do not cultivate dhyāna;

they take no pleasure in it nor rejoice in it. They speak falsely and with inverted views, their natures are evil, harsh, and violent, and they are beset by many obstacles. Lacking wisdom, they do not love or delight in meditative concentration for even a single kṣaṇa. This is called the ‘peg-word’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) by which all sentient beings are fully possessed of craving?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“All sentient beings are fully possessed by craving; afflictions arise in abundance, they lack a heart of joy, do not delight in tranquility, and do not practice equanimity. Yet, regarding the nature of craving, they have no awakening and do not attain bodhi; this is called the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ by which all sentient beings are fully possessed of anger?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“All sentient beings are fully endowed with and dwell in anger; they are fully endowed with the very nature of anger. This is called the ‘Pile-Driver Phrase.’”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what way is the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) fully possessed by all sentient beings through their ignorance?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“When all sentient beings do not seek the Buddha-dharma, when they possess all forms of pride and all their conduct is non-brahmacarya, and when they abide in the equality of delusion and abide in the essential nature of delusion, failing to train in bodhi—this is called the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that the stake-sentence is fully present within the deluded bodies of all sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"All sentient beings dwell in ignorance within their bodies; they do not recite any dharmas, nor do they believe in or read the sūtras. By nature they are evil and full of resentment, taking no pleasure in the Mahāyāna, and remaining settled in the most supreme unwholesomeness—this is called the 'stake-word' (kīla-pada)."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) by which all sentient beings are fully possessed of false views?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “All sentient beings possess false views;

they take refuge in the ten-bodied Buddha, which is not a true refuge. They constantly commit the ten non-virtues and practice the ten false views, yet they do not awaken to these false views. Delighting in their inherent nature, they dwell securely amidst the five desires, dwell securely amidst greed, hatred, and delusion, and dwell securely in obstructions. Thus they fail to attain bodhi; this is called the ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada).”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is this ‘stake-word’ (kīla-pada) by which all sentient beings dwell and listen to the Dharma?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"All sentient beings, listen with single-minded reverence; I shall speak for you.
All sentient beings who truly seek the Dharma should be single-minded and unmoving, free from fear and dread. The merit of the Buddha is vast and great, yet the foolish do not know it."
I possess true words of instruction, yet you do not give rise to reverence, nor do you dwell securely in listening and receiving them;

instead, you dwell in equanimity toward greed, dwell in equanimity toward anger, dwell in equanimity toward delusion, dwell in equanimity amidst the five desires, dwell in equanimity toward obstacles and hindrances, and dwell in equanimity toward attachment and delight. You do not praise the Buddha, who possesses such unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

nor do you praise the liberation of such unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which consists of dwelling in the essential nature of greed, dwelling in the essential nature of anger, dwelling in the essential nature of delusion, dwelling in the essential nature of the five desires, dwelling in the essential nature of obstacles and hindrances, and dwelling in the essential nature of attachment and delight.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If you had not asked, I would not have spoken for you; since you now ask me, I shall explain it to you.
All wholesome dharmas should be studied, for the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is perfectly and equally endowed with all wholesome dharmas."

Thus, with the spiritual teachers and virtuous friends rejoicing, one studies the Mahāyāna teachings and practices the Mahāyāna path, possessing great power; having abandoned all else, there is nothing remaining.

With single-minded resolve, one makes vows to seek the supreme Dharma, applying oneself with diligent focus to contemplate the realm of the Tathāgatas of the five wisdoms. Since the realm of the Tathāgatas has no separate realms and all realms are equal, one thus studies the Dharma day and night with a single mind, making offerings.

Mañjuśrī! If sentient beings seek the Dharma in this way, they shall attain the Bodhi of a Buddha and fully comprehend the wholesome dharmas; all wholesome dharmas are complete in this manner. If one does not study the Buddha-dharma, one is truly no different from birds and beasts.
