At that time, the Devaputra Padmavikrīḍita, together with ten thousand devaputras, all came to make offerings to the World-Honored One and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.

Each holding exquisite and famous flowers—udumbara flowers, blue lotuses, white lotuses, māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers—they gave rise to a heart of reverence and, with various words, joyfully praised the World-Honored One and Mañjuśrī:

“Disliking worldly pleasures, he transcends the three realms; his mind is free from afflictions and devoid of all evils. His speech is truthful, profoundly truthful; it is the auspiciousness of the *dharmadhātu*, the auspiciousness of truth, the auspiciousness of the subtle and wondrous, the countless, supreme, and foremost auspiciousness.”
Thus did the devaputra praise the World-Honored One and Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputra Padmavikrīḍita:
"Among all the devaputras, you have attained the foremost rank!"

The Son of Heaven, regarding his own body both internally and externally, maintains a mind free from discrimination; he attains the most supreme and foremost Dharma, the most supreme among the multitude, the most subtle and foremost, the most exquisitely wonderful and foremost. Abiding in the midst of the great assembly with a true mind, he is able to make the most supreme offerings and thereby attain the foremost state.
The Buddha said,
“Devaputra! If you were without greed, hatred, and delusion, and did not give rise to afflictions, then being thus would be no different from that of an ordinary person.”

If a son of heaven indulges in strife and combat, he loses the path to Bodhi. If he loves and delights in all dharmas—the Buddha-dharmas of a Bodhisattva—and joyfully cultivates the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

such a son of heaven has planted roots of goodness in past lives, has reverently made offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, remains far removed from all evils, and his mind radiates light. Diligently studying the Buddha-dharma, he manifests light because he dwells skillfully in the practices of the ten stages; he studies the teachings of the Buddha with courageous delight.
If one does not thus delight in the Buddha-dharma, but engages in much contention and dispute, failing to give rise to a heart of offering, their wisdom will be meager and thin.

Thus, this devaputra, with a mind of haughty pride, takes no delight in any dharmas and does not associate with virtuous friends. This devaputra is despised by the assembly; he is not in harmony with bodhi, lacks a heart of reverence, treats the Triple Gem with contempt, and does not study the teachings, being no different from a fool.

With profound reverence for the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they seek the perfection of all-knowledge and attain the conduct of celestial sons, dwelling securely among the virtuous assembly.
Those celestial sons do not abide in greed, do not abide in hatred, do not abide in delusion; they have no attachment to the necessities of life and do not practice wrong views.
With reverence, they inquire after the Well-Gone One and Mañjuśrī, prostrating and making offerings, remaining entirely free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
“The World-Honored One speaks according to the truth, and the devaputra delights in and abides according to the truth.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying: “You abide securely in the Mahāyāna, practicing no deviant conduct and holding no deviant views.”

Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the sons of the gods went to the place where Mañjuśrī was, praising and making offerings to him; they studied all dharmas, attaining perfection in non-discrimination and being free from any deviant conduct.

At that time, ten thousand devaputras heard the Buddha, amidst the great assembly, preach the Dharma of non-arising patience and its peaceful abiding; they all cultivated the conduct of Mañjuśrī and attained the most supreme and wondrous Dharma.

Having realized that form is fundamentally empty through the adamantine phrases, secret phrases, and wedge-phrases, and that its essential nature is not deviant and free from contention, they attained the Dharma of bodhi-liberation. Thereupon, they paid respectful offerings, practiced meditative concentration, maintained, recited, proclaimed, and transcribed [the teachings].

By thus perfuming themselves with these five dharmas, all people were filled with joy, their three karmas became pure, and they attained peaceful and blissful practice through the complete proclamation of all dharmas and all Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Devaputra Lotus Play, saying:

"Regarding such sounds and forms, foolish bodhisattvas—neither delighting in the Buddha-dharma of this life nor the future life, craving external sounds and external forms, neither fearing nor being terrified by them—become attached and deluded by all sounds; they possess no merit."

Thus spoke the Blessed One. The Devaputra Padmavikrīḍita praised him, moving to and fro through the sky, manifesting various transformations and wondrous sounds produced by the roots of goodness and meritorious deeds of past lives. Having attained the Bodhi of the Buddha, born into a noble lineage, endowed with perfect etiquette, and perfected in meritorious karma, he had fully realized and mastered all qualities of form and sound.
The World-Honored One declared:

"You shall be born as a son of heaven. For as many true *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas as there are, you shall honor, revere, and make offerings to Dharma-preachers; you shall possess all peace and happiness, with clothing, food, bedding, meals, and medicinal decoctions, as well as various such superior and exquisite incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments, provided day and night without interruption, all fully complete.
Abiding within the Dharma, you shall resolutely seek supreme and excellent karmic rewards, free from all anger."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Having fully realized form and sound, you shall swiftly attain all peace and happiness throughout as many *gaṅgā*-sands of eons as there are Bodhisattvas.
During those *gaṅgā*-sand eons, that Devaputra will not give rise to afflictions; his mind will be free from arrogance, and he will perfect the true flavor of the Dharma teachings.

Thus, the devaputra gave rise to a resolute mind; hearing the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma, he fully understood sounds and forms, became free from all suffering and affliction, and was likewise free from slander. Rejoicing and praising, he attained the supreme peace and happiness of all.
The Buddha said, “Devaputra!

Now all people do not seek the Buddha-dharma; they are greedily attached to the necessities of life and feel neither dread nor fear. They are not like the worldly people of King Śāla, whose roots of goodness have matured.”
When the World-Honored One had spoken thus, the Devaputra Padmavikrīḍita, having heard this sound of the Dharma, realized the essential nature of form and entered deeply into the Buddha’s wisdom.
“If sentient beings do not study the Buddha-dharma, do not cultivate meditative concentration, and take no pleasure in nor inquire about any phenomena, this is not the practice of a bodhisattva.”

“They constantly harbor evil thoughts, do not study right wisdom, and upon hearing the voices of women, they feel love, delight, and greedy attachment, having no fear of the karmic consequences of their sins!
After the World-Honored One had spoken, the Devaputra Lotus-Play said:

“The Bodhisattva-devaputras have distracted bodies and minds; they do not receive the teachings of the World-Honored One, and their three karmas are unwholesome. They slander the hearing of the Dharma, dwelling on sounds with greed, dwelling on sounds with anger, and dwelling on sounds with delusion. They do not draw near to virtuous friends, do not study the Buddha-dharma, and are greedily attached to women without ever feeling satiety.”

They do not learn the sound of joy, nor the sound of delighting in sensual pleasures; they take pleasure in listening to the voices of evil people, and do not learn the voices of virtuous people, nor the sound of writing, nor the voice of the Buddha. Greedily attached to female beauty, they are always like drunken men;

they do not learn the sound of peace and happiness, nor the sound of leaving the household life; they delight in the sound of wisdom-less teachings, taking pleasure in hearing the voices of non-Buddhists, and longing for the voices of women.

They do not study the sound of the Buddha-dharma regarding generosity; they do not study the sound of the Buddha-dharma regarding ethical discipline; they do not study the sound of the Buddha-dharma regarding patience; they do not study the sound of the Buddha-dharma regarding diligence; they do not study the sound of the Buddha-dharma regarding meditative concentration; they do not study the sound of the Buddha-dharma regarding wisdom. Instead, they are attached to the voices of women, seek out indulgence from afar, and associate with evil friends. They do not study the voices of virtuous people but are attached to worldly sounds, never ceasing day or night, and thus fail to attain nirvāṇa.
Attached to women, they do not study the Buddha-dharma and thus fail to attain liberation;

instead, they wander through villages and settlements, giving rise to attachment from birth, constantly indulging in pleasure with women. They do not associate with virtuous friends, nor do they practice the Mahāyāna, the conduct of a bhikṣu, or the righteous conduct of a layperson; they follow only the path of error.
They walk only upon the paths of women and take delight at hearing the voices of women;
they do not give rise to reverence upon hearing the voice of the Buddha, nor do they cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), but instead dwell securely in afflictions (kleśa).
They disturb and confuse the masses, practicing the ways of external paths (tīrthika), and thus lack the fruits of merit.
They do not train in the practice of upholding the precepts, but instead cling to the practice of breaking them;
their fundamental nature is inferior, and they cling to that inferior nature;

they do not associate with virtuous friends and do not train in the Buddha-dharma, but instead cling to greed and fail to train in the Buddha-dharma, cling to anger and fail to train in the Buddha-dharma, and cling to delusion and fail to train in the Buddha-dharma.
Foolish and ignorant, they do not accept instruction; their minds are congested and unable to comprehend.

They do not study the practices of the Buddhas, nor the practices of Bodhisattvas, nor the practices of Śrāvakas. Regarding the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they neither inquire nor study; with deeply heavy karmic obstructions, they depart and distance themselves to commit unwholesome deeds.
They are greedily attached to female forms; their minds are deluded by their own actions, and they are withered by afflictions.
Lacking faith in true bodhi, they drift further and further away from it and are loathed by all people.
Such persons are greedily attached to female beauty; they obtain neither peace nor happiness, nor do they find tranquility.
They neither prostrate nor show reverence, and failing to awaken themselves, they shall not attain bodhi.
If a Bodhisattva-devaputra diligently cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action, making them truly perfect, and accumulates roots of goodness with a heart full of joy;

this Bodhisattva-devaputra shall go to where other Bodhisattva-devaputras who are widely learned and possess great erudition reside, there to cultivate all roots of goodness until they are fully perfected, thereby eliminating karmic obstructions and attaining purity of mind.

"Once the karmic obstructions have been removed, body and mind become light and serene; one remains far removed from all desires, and throughout day and night, no further thought of women arises, as one dwells peacefully in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The ocean of the Buddhas' Dharma is boundless; its subtle forms and appearances cannot be perceived, and its subtle sounds, its sounds of joy, and its sounds of supreme delight cannot be heard.

With single-minded focus, one cultivates the subtle Buddha-nature, remains far removed from obstructive defilements, reaches the other shore, and dwells securely in the Dharma—neither dwelling in nirvana nor in the villages, neither going nor coming, and free from [the notions of] giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Free from anger, free from greed, hatred, and delusion, all are entirely equal.
World-Honored One!
You have spoken this truly subtle Dharma-gate according to its meaning.
The Buddha said:

“The Devaputra Padmavikrīḍita of Great Wisdom and the Youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī—these two great beings have planted roots of goodness in the past, throughout immeasurable, incalculable, and asāṃkhyeya kalpas across the buddha-fields. They have heard and received the teachings, cultivated the practices of the Mahāyāna, severed all karmic obstructions, and possess profound and deep-rooted merit from former lives, having accumulated boundless and limitless virtues.”
Having obtained this meritorious retribution through past causes and conditions, there is truly no one who can rival him within this assembly.

Thus, the Devaputra Padmavikrīḍita, having distanced himself from forms and sounds, with a mind of absolute sincerity, made offerings of various exquisite incenses, flowers, lamps, candles, and rare, wonderful foods and drinks that surpassed all others. Drawing near to the Buddha’s voice, he listened as Mañjuśrī expounded the profound, equal, and true Dharma-gate.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

“In a past kalpa, within my Dharma, you thoroughly understood such forms and sounds as the supreme marks; all karmic obstructions were entirely removed from you, and you dwelt securely in meritorious deeds, with ten thousand virtues fully perfected, such that none could surpass you, even including the Bodhisattvas of the past.”
Mañjuśrī said: "In this way, I have fully understood the karmic obstacles of form, the karmic obstacles of anger, and all karmic obstacles of evil; I shall remain far removed from them all.

I will resolutely protect myself and attend upon the World-Honored One as he has taught, remaining free from all defiled dharmas, attaining pure meritorious karma, and having a mind free from afflictions."

In my past lives, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I gave rise to the vast mind and cultivated meritorious deeds; I contemplated and brought to perfection the fullness of virtuous conduct.

Thus, through the practice of the past, I now receive this retribution: I have encountered the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Siṃhaghoṣeśvararāja.
The lifespan of that Buddha was immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of years, and he was fully known by all beings of the triple world.

The world was named Great Radiance; in that Buddha-land, there were many jewel trees, with paths demarcated by golden cords and lined with rows of jewel trees. When fragrant breezes blew, the branches and leaves brushed against one another, producing wondrous sounds. These sounds proclaimed the sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of non-arising, the sound of non-ceasing, the sound of formlessness, and the sound of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Upon hearing such sounds, sentient beings all attained liberation.

"At that time, that Tathāgata had an assembly of twenty-seven koṭis of śrāvakas who all came to listen to the Dharma. This great community of bhikṣus had severed all afflictions, laid down their heavy burdens, and attained liberation through wisdom and liberation of mind; these bhikṣus, with undistracted minds, went back and forth to listen to the Dharma and seek the Bodhi of the Buddha."

That Tathāgata further had an assembly of twenty-seven koṭis as well as a great community of bhikṣus, all of whom came to listen and receive the teachings, shouldering the burden of the Tathāgata’s instruction, and having attained liberation through wisdom and liberation of mind.
In this way, bodhisattvas from other directions all came to hear the Dharma, each attaining all dharmas of patience and becoming fully endowed with peace and happiness.
Likewise, from the buddha-fields of the ten directions, countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of buddhas all came to hear the Dharma.

Upon hearing of the Ānanda-bahudhātuka-dhāraṇī-samādhi, countless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings attained tranquil peace and happiness; their hearts were filled with joy, and they discussed it among themselves, resolving that from their past lives until this present one, they would seek nothing else, but would remain steadfastly established as Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the Tathāgata proclaimed the sublime Dharma in that land; when all was concluded, the True Dharma remained in the world for sixty hundred thousand years.
Then, that Tathāgata further expounded the teachings of all Bodhisattvas—praised by all people and characterized by a mind free from external conditions—to the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya.

In past kalpas, this bodhisattva cultivated the bodhisattva-dharma, dwelling in the purification of the path. He took no delight in any worldly dharmas; his faculties were undisturbed, and he attained profound liberation. Regarding the true, supreme, and wondrous Dharma, he fully understood its characteristics and forms. He spoke with joy and exultation, dedicating himself single-mindedly to transcribing it. He engaged in discussion and debate with virtuous friends, yet he did not speak to non-humans, fearing they might give rise to slander.

Yet those sentient beings dwell in attachment to all phenomena through the nature of greed, dwell in attachment to all phenomena through the nature of hatred, and dwell in attachment to all phenomena through the nature of delusion.

This Bodhisattva delights solely in all Buddha-dharmas and does not delight in any worldly dharmas. It is not through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings that they take delight, but rather they delight only in the practice of Bodhi and various virtuous deeds. With a mind free from discrimination, they constantly practice patience, being without greed or anger, and without notions of right or wrong; they dwell securely in the profound Dharma-realm of the Tathāgata.
"At that time, there was another bhikṣu named Jayamati who delighted in bodhi.
Then the World-Honored One expounded for him all the sublime dharmas; he attained the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the twelve dhūta virtues, and constantly practiced these deeds."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Vijayamati:
“The bodhisattva who has stilled all the sense faculties thoroughly understands all supreme practices.
Having heard what the Buddha said, the bhikṣu Vijayamati joined his palms to receive the teaching; he withdrew to a secluded place, dwelt in tranquility, and cultivated all supreme practices.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya gave rise to a vast and boundless mind; carrying his alms bowl through the royal city, he guided sentient beings, teaching them as he went from door to door. He begged for food at the houses of elders, householders, and virtuous friends. Those wise people who encountered him felt joy in their hearts, making offerings and praising him.

Yet, when some householders or virtuous friends spoke with harsh words or slandered him, he did not give rise to ill will. Content with little speech, his words were true and his conduct sincere; his heart harbored no anger toward others, and his countenance was always gentle and pleasant. Consequently, those householders and virtuous friends praised him."

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya expounded upon all phenomena of form (*rūpadharma*), many among the community of monks did not understand them; they fell into various false views, dwelling in seclusion and minor matters, obstructed by attachment and pride, obstructed by aversion and pride, obstructed by delusion and pride, and obstructed by their craving for all phenomena, such that they would not listen to his true words and deeds.
The Bodhisattva Quieting the Faculties further exhorted lay practitioners and virtuous friends that they must not succumb to afflictions nor commit various evil deeds.

Householder, though you have a virtuous friend, you are unable to practice the conduct of patience; you go yourself to places of greed and places of great greed, and you go to the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, giving rise to five kinds of slander:
namely, love, delight, craving, anger, and delusion, because the mind is full of afflictions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya was wandering through the royal city to teach and transform others. He spoke with the householder Kalyāṇamitra, praising the bhikṣu Jayamati, saying: "He is a true member of the Saṃgha whom all people should honor. He no longer dwells in the royal city but has retired to a place of tranquility to abide there; furthermore, he takes no pleasure in the offerings of incense and flowers at monasteries, and most bhikṣus do not delight in seeing him."

This Bhikṣu Śreṣṭhamati is a true spiritual friend; the community of bhikṣus has deeply entered into wrong views, and being obstructed by greed, anger, and delusion, they are unable to distance themselves from the obstructions of various evil karmas.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said: "The community of bhikṣus does not study the wholesome dharmas, does not practice any forms of contemplation, does not study the profound and sublime Dharma, and does not seek awakening."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya spoke these verses for the community of bhikṣus:
"If there be greed, hatred, or delusion, And one does not cultivate the practice of enlightenment—
Since enlightenment has a nature free from greed, One should distance oneself from all such things."
Fools do not realize this; they are addicted to various sensual pleasures.
Lacking the tranquility of dhyāna, they cannot proceed to the Buddha-land.
Arrogant and heedless, they possess not even a fraction of merit.
Regarding the pure precepts of all Buddhas, they give rise to a mind of doubt;
through greedy attachment they commit various evils, and thus lack the Jewels of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Even if they study written words, their minds are full of clever artifice.
Regarding true enlightenment, how does one attain liberation?
A person who studies enlightenment is free from afflictions and conceptual discrimination;
by cultivating the visualization of the Buddha, they attain the perfection of right view.
Unable to understand the Dharma, sentient beings fall into wrong views;
they distance themselves from the Buddha’s teachings and abide in greed, hatred, and delusion.
They do not show respect or prostrate, nor do they draw near to the Dharma masters.
Afflicted by suffering, they give rise to discrimination and lack a mind of forbearance.
Deluded, they do not know themselves; out of folly they commit various evils.
They remain far removed from the Buddha-way and do not accept the exhortations and transformations of others.
One will swiftly attain awakening; if a person possesses patience, they enter the realm of equanimous liberation.
Transcending the world, their eye perceives all things with wisdom;
contemplate and visualize the dharma of patience.
And attaining the Buddha’s bodhi, by dwelling securely therein,
they will certainly be free from demonic activities; with the power of meditative concentration manifesting before them,
having thus attained liberation, they proceed to the realm of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings who diligently study the Dharma Are truly beyond measure;
They attain the state of neither arising nor ceasing, Because they are free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Though they travel through various villages and towns, They remain without a mind of discrimination.
If someone slanders them, they feel no anger;
if they encounter someone praising them, they likewise feel no joy.
Abiding securely in the Buddha’s Bodhi, they regard all things with complete equanimity.
The Buddha-dharma is like space, for it cannot be measured.
The unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddhas—fools do not awaken to it;
failing to cultivate the contemplation of tranquility, they are not liberated therein.
Sentient beings crave negligence and lack the resolve to train in the Noble Path;
they gallop after the pleasures of desire, no different from madmen.
Foolish and lacking tranquility, they are unwilling to study for enlightenment.
How does one become free from karmic obstructions?
By distancing oneself from all sensual pleasures and devoting oneself single-mindedly to the practice of dhyāna,
one becomes the foremost among the assembly.
Practicing upon the true path, they constantly mind the Bodhi of the Buddhas without further conceptual discrimination.
With a heart of genuine love and joy for the supreme path of Bodhi, both dragons and devas rejoice.
Abiding securely in the virtues of the Buddha, they give rise to no unwholesome thoughts regarding the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
seeking only the Bodhi of the Buddha, they learn nothing else. Therefore, within this assembly,
Virtuous conduct is the foremost.
Though one may study various non-Buddhist paths or engage in worldly occupations and affairs,
these are not equal to cultivating the roots of all that is wholesome within the Buddha-dharma.
Delighting in their kin and craving their worldly possessions,
they do not seek the Buddha’s bodhi; fond of worldly glory and honor,
there is not even for a single moment when they study the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
They frequently give rise to conceptual thoughts and dwell securely in various sensual pleasures;
yet the nature of desire is fundamentally illusory, like a mirage or an echo in a valley.
Out of folly they remain entirely unaware, and their minds constantly give birth to self-conceit.
They do not praise the Buddha’s bodhi, for in reality there is neither knowledge nor vision.
Failing to understand the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena, they stubbornly cling to them as existent;
yet both the conditioned and the unconditioned are entirely equal.
If sentient beings understand this clearly and diligently cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna,
proceeding toward the path of the Buddha’s Bodhi, they are no longer ordinary worldlings.
Abiding securely within the Dharma, they shall obtain the heart-seal of all Buddhas.
Having perfected the karma of merit, one is no different from a Buddha.
Yet, if a single thought of greed arises, one commits a pārājika offense;
if that greedy mind is not severed, one will be entangled and bound by it.
Reluctant to guard the *śīla*, lacking meditative concentration and contemplation,
they feel no joy upon seeing the Buddha; having committed various evils throughout the long night,
they fall into the hells and undergo the retribution of their sins for *koṭi* eons.
Because of this violation of the precepts, one does not understand even a small portion of the Dharma;
how then could one attain Bodhi?
Such a person is no different from a fool.
If one performs meritorious deeds, yet the mind is not pure and sincere,
does not cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna, and lacks meditative concentration and contemplation—
how can such a person obtain the seal of the Unsurpassed Dharma King?

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya had spoken these verses for the community of bhikṣus, three thousand two hundred devas and humans attained the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*), and eighty thousand bhikṣus, having heard the Dharma, each attained liberation;
furthermore, that bhikṣu Vijñāta attained purity of the three karmas and was freed from the obstruction of karma.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has proclaimed the profound meaning of the Dharma; though I contemplate it day and night, the merits of the ten titles of the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing dharmas are difficult for foolish persons to measure."

The Tathāgata’s dharma of non-arising patience is likewise difficult to measure; the meaning of the dharma taught by the Tathāgata is inconceivable, and it is one and the same teaching as the meaning of the dharmas in my own mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the true meaning of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, in the final five hundred years, many people will have no faith, will not feel dread, and will not be terrified; even the devas shall be likewise.”

I shall resolutely approach and make offerings to the Dharma-meaning of the Tathāgata; I shall give away my body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, praising and chanting in homage during the three periods of the day; I shall dwell in and further expound the Dharma-meaning throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and with voices like those of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I shall cause them to hear and attain the Dharma of patience, thereby dwelling in the Dharma-meaning.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard the meaning of all the Buddha’s teachings, accepted and upheld them with faith, vowing to proclaim them in turn for the sake of others.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Siṃhavikrīḍita Bodhisattva, Padmavikrīḍita Bodhisattva, and the assembly of great bodhisattvas such as Satyaka, together with an incalculable number of bhikṣus, the Venerable Ānanda, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they paid homage and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Proclamation of All Dharmas According to the Mahāyāna, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll II.
